newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Russia Gazprom offer attractive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia Gazprom offer attractive.

text.p: The price for an international offering for the world's largest natural gas producer, Russia's RAO Gazprom, was indicated at the equivalent of $1.40-$1.60 per share on Monday, a level analysts said should ensure the deal is a success.
"It seems likely it will go well. Gazprom should be accepted by a much wider audience of investors than the usual Russian stock," said a senior fund manager based in London.

The 23.7 million American Depositary Shares (ADS) on offer in this landmark Russia deal each represent 10 common shares, and the size of the issue could be increased to 27.255 million ADS if demand is sufficient, lead managers Morgan Stanley and Dresdner Kleinwort Benson said.
This would allow Gazprom to raise up to $436 million.

Foreign investors are being asked to stump up more than four times the 33.5 cents Russians pay for Gazprom's underying shares for a dollar denominated security which avoids direct exposure to the rouble hassles of directly owning a Russian share.
There is an additional incentive as despite being the largest company in Russia, it is one of the most thinly traded on the Moscow bourse as Gazprom imposes restrictions on trading.
"I am never going to really understand Gazprom. I feel comfortable with what I am being told at a price of around $1.50 per share," the fund manager said.
At $1.50 per share, the ADS issue values Gazprom at $36 billion, compared with the current market capitalisation of $12.0 billion for Russia's entire oil and gas industry.

For this, foreign investors are getting a slice of Russia which is closer to the government than any other company -- Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin used to run Gazprom and the new Russian energy minister is a former manager.

They are also getting one to one and a half percent of a company which produces 559.5 billion cubic metres of natural gas a year, supplied 21 percent of western Europe's demand in 1995 and has 23 percent of global reserves.
"This is a unique opportunity to own Gazprom if you do not have direct access to the Russian equity market," said a leading oil analyst.

Russia's inclusion in the International Finance Corporation's emerging markets index will also boost interest in Gazprom as investors use the index to allocate assets and it is also seen as an endorsement of emerging share markets. "Fund managers in have money coming out of their ears and we are willing to overlook certain things," said one.
However, there are flies in the ointment.
The issue was first mooted two years ago in a deal from Kleinwort Benson but was delayed when the Russian share market collapsed in the wake of the Mexican financial crisis in 1994.
There was confusion about how much the company wished to raise as Gazprom officials had believed that they could get $25 billion for a nine percent stake in the company.
Western investors are worried that if they still plan nine percent, the market could be flooded with new issues, which would depress the price.
"There should be a commitment that they are not going to sell new shares for six to twelve months," said a fund manager.
Also, the kind of investor who gets shares will affect their price in the after-market.

"If hedge funds or short term investors get their hands on it, there will be a lively aftermarket but that is no good for long term investors like myself who will simply ignore Morgan Stanley's future offerings if we get stung this time round," said one potential investor.
